newsitem.title: SPAIN: Moody's upgrade confirms comeback at Spain's BCH.
newsitem.headline: Moody's upgrade confirms comeback at Spain's BCH.

text.p: U.S. rating agency Moody's upgraded its outlook for Spain's Banco Central Hispanoamericano (BCH) to stable from negative on Monday, consigning the bank's troubles to the past.
Moody's said the change reflected "the improvement in the balance sheet's quality and the efforts to reduce the operating costs and to rearrange industrial investments."

For BCH a product of the 1991 merger of Banco Central and Banco Hispanoamericano, the upbeat assessment underscored the view that the bank's sweeping restructuring and rationalisation efforts had purged its loan problems.
"It's very positive," said Lola Ybarra, banking analyst at Banco Santander in Madrid. "It confirms that the problems with non-performing loans have been solved."

Central Hispano, Spain's fourth largest bank in terms of assets, has struggled with the impact of bad loans that forced it to provision 700 billion pesetas in the first years of the decade, causing a profit slump.
Its slow progress, despite a large customer base known for its loyalty, contributed to periodic speculation it would merge with or be absorbed by other banks in the highly competitive Spanish market.
But recent earnings improvement has led the market to reassess Central Hispano.
"We agree with (Moody's) criterion. The trend for the bank is positive. There's no doubt there is more confidence," another Madrid-based analyst said.
In late October, Central Hispano presented solid and well-received nine-month results showing a 20 percent increase in attributable profits to 27.31 billion pesetas.
Furthermore analysts said they expected profits to improve next year thanks to expansion in Latin America. BCH most recently added a stake in Banco de Colombia to its interests.
Earlier this month, Central Hispano sold its 49.9 percent stake in Spanish sugar producer Azucarera, as part of a revamp of its holdings.

The bank is expected to invest the profits from the sale in increasing its stake in electricity group Endesa to three percent from 1.5 percent and would also channel funds into Retevision, Spain's second domestic telephone operator.

As a result of the changes Central Hispano's stock, which has dramatically underperformed in the past few years, began to pick up mid-summer from 2,410 pesetas and had risen to 3,160 at the close of trading on Friday.
